segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m happy to see you for a second time to speak with me. To start with, I’m going to remind you why we do this. The kids go to school on one side here and the adults have school on the other side. They will one day listen to how Cherokee was spoken well. Another reason is if you have kids or grandkids, they may want to listen in the future. They may let them do that one day. To start with, can you say your full English name?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Now?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Harry Daugherty.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Aniyosg.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I was born here in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I always knew you as Dinatli.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did you get that name?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t know. They used to call me that when I was a kid.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your real name is Aniyosg?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Aniyosg. I have never heard anyone call me that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Not Aniyosg. Just Dinatli?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes, and Slim.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Slim. My grandchild called you Slim when they talked about you.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. In some communities they wouldn’t know who you were talking about if you said Harry. If you said, “Slim,” they wouldn’t know either in some places. It happened to Sam. Someone asked him how Harry was doing and he said, “I don’t know. I don’t know who that is.” He said they just looked at him. They said, “Then what about Slim? Do you know him?” “Yeah, I know him.” [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did you get the name Slim?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We used to play baseball when we were boys, and someone called me that and it just caught on.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So that’s how it started?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah. That’s how it started and it stuck with me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you play ball in the Bell area?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes, but I grew up in the Oak Ridge area though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Out there?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. There’s not a house there anymore. It burned down a long time ago. I do have land there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have some there?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you live when you used to come to our house?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Killer Mountain. Do you know where Snow Gonzales used to live?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We used to live there (borrowed). I used to live with my aunt then. She took us in. I don’t really remember my mother. That’s what she would do. Just have different people come pick me up and I would stay with them. Letsili was her name, the woman that came to get us and took us in. That’s where we lived and we would come down the hill to come to your mom’s house.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I remember that. I don’t remember Sam coming over much, but he might have been there.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He was there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, he was there?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who is older? You?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I’m older than Sam. Sam and Nell were the youngest. The oldest one’s name was Man.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t think I knew him.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He didn’t ever go there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Okay.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He grew up on the hill.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When did you leave Oak Ridge?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We left when my mom passed away. She was sickly. She had the TB (Tuberculosis). She was always at Talihina. That’s why I don’t remember her much.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: She would come back sometimes. When she passed away, we, the kids, were by ourselves. The adults didn’t like that we were living in the house by ourselves. We went to live with my aunt where my uncle used to live. After that we all went our separate ways. I grew up someplace different than Sam and Nell did. We moved to Texas from there. When we moved, I went to school in Texas for a while. Then we came back. My uncle was here from California. He said that he always wanted a boy and he had all girls. I couldn’t say anything to refuse because I was so young, so they took me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I was 12 years old.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t want to go.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I grew up in California. I left from there when I was 18. I said I was old enough. I did go to school there in Oakland, California. I lived there for six years. When I became an adult, then I came back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did you get back?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: By bus.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did it take you?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Probably three days. I missed a bus somewhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I think it was three days though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Back up the hill. There were a lot of people in the area then. There were houses in any direction. I was staying here and there and working. I had to work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you do for work?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I was working in Arkansas in a chicken place with chicken catchers. I told them I didn’t want to chase and catch chickens until I was old. There were some guys there that worked in construction. They were living in Missouri. I asked them if they would hire me if I went there. They said they been needing some workers but hadn’t found any yet. I told them I would go. I went to Cameron, Missouri. I was helping Tom Bearpaw. He was there so I helped him. We were laying telephone lines underground. I was there less than six months then they put me on a backhoe. I really liked that. I worked there for 15 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Backhoe?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes, that’s what I used.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t break any waterlines did you?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Nah. We just went everywhere. I’d get calls from everywhere. We used to go to Texas, just anywhere. We moved around a lot. That’s what we did. Have you heard of Newman Briggs?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, I have heard of him.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He was in Minnesota with another crew. I don’t know what he did, but he was a worker. I was staying in Abilene, and I was ready to come back to Oklahoma at Christmas for vacation. Newman Briggs called and said for me to go up there for the winter. We argued about it for a while. They told me that I had to go there to run a backhoe for them because someone had quit. They thought I had a license! I got in my truck and loaded up the backhoe and headed out. I went by on my way up. I kept looking back this direction. Then went through interstate in Oklahoma City. I finally made it to Pequot Lakes, Minnesota.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: With no license?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No license. And in the company truck. I had credit cards for hotels and food. It didn’t cost me anything and they paid me for traveling. There were just a few things that were dangerous when traveling. Roadblocks. One time I was coming back through Arkansas. I didn’t like 71 Highway. They put roadblocks anytime and anywhere. They had one somewhere on the way back. Boy, my heart was pounding coming through there. About the fourth car going through there they flagged it down. So, I just went right on by. The cops were busy so the rest of us kept going. I joined in with them and drove on through. I met up with the others in Joplin, [Missouri]. Then we got to Kirkville, Missouri. I went everywhere without a license.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When did you get your license, if you got one?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I got one in Stilwell when I was about 20 years old. Back in ’71, I got a DUI in Abilene and they took my license away. I didn’t pay so I told them to keep it. I was in jail for about three months. I told them to leave me here and I would just stay here. They took my car, but one of my friends came and got it and kept it at his house. He used to come visit me sometimes. When I got released, he told me my car was at his house. I went there and he told me someone was looking for me. I told him, “I don’t care.” There was one woman that I lived with for a while, but it wasn’t working out. She wanted to boss me around about everything. One morning I told her I was going to the store and that I would be back in a while. She’s probably still standing there waiting on me to this day!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You just left and didn’t go back?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, I just looked at that store and drove on by!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She’s probably still standing there by herself!

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: She’s probably getting old standing there by herself! I got to the house about dark. I used to have a ’57 Ford, but I made it back just fine. [God] was looking out for me back then. I still believe that even now and when I was going everywhere. Running around Stilwell!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You do have a license though?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No? [laughs]

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Most of Stilwell knows that I don’t have one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They think, “That’s Harry and he doesn’t have a license.”

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: They wave and I just drive on by.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I worked in Fayetteville, Arkansas as a finisher while building bridges. There was a black man, and he told me that he found a woman. He said, “Boy, Chief, when I got home, she had my bath water ready. We would sit down and watch TV. When we decided to take a bath, she would get the water ready again. When I got up in the morning, she would get it ready again!” He said boy, I’m just going to vanish! He said he did the same as you said you did. He left for work and he didn’t go back. He said she’s probably still waiting for him.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: That’s what I thought too. I was thinking that I’m not going to be bossed around by a woman. She was doing good for me. It was just that one thing. She wanted me to do whatever she thought I should do. It wasn’t going to be that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you do when you came back?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I just got back in construction for a while, then the company fell apart. It was K and B out of Tulsa that was my employer. It was R. P. Kennan[?] and James Bolten [?] R. P. Kennan retired and left it to the other one. When the other one took over, he wanted all of us to start at the bottom of pay. I told them I didn’t want to do that, so I quit. I came back. I don’t know for sure when, but I came back. I started working just anywhere then. I got tired of that, so I went to Fort Smith and worked there for a while. Somebody had a car and he asked me if I wanted to move away from here with them and I told him that I didn’t think his car would make it anywhere. He said, “Well I’m going to leave it here.” We were looking for some thick clothes. We caught a box car. There I was in a box car riding like it was a Cadillac. We switched out in Baxter Springs, Kansas. One was going to Kansas City area where the trains meet. We got on and by three or four in the afternoon, we got to Dalhart, Texas. We caught a ride with someone with a car and left.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you know where you were going?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No. We were just out to see what it was like, was what I thought. I didn’t really care. When we left there, then we got to Portland, Oregon. We all went separate ways there. I caught a ride with a truck driver. I went to Seattle and then I left there and went to Pasco, Washington. I just got a ride with someone. I went to what’s that called? Rescue Mission? They had one of those and it was huge but there were also a lot of people there. I went there for a place to sleep and eat. They told me to write my name down. They said they could give me a cleaning job there and I could stay there. They said the other workers were useless. They were supposed to sweep around but instead they would grab a broom for a short time then run outside. That’s what I did for a while. Everyone back home was wondering where I went like Sam and Man and all of my family. They didn’t know where I was. They thought I went to North Carolina. I used to talk about going there a lot. They never wanted me to go, so they assumed that was where I was. I called Sam for no reason. It was evening here and it was about midnight there. There’s two hours difference in time. I talked to Diane, Sam’s wife, for a while. I asked her where Sam was and she said he’s in a truck somewhere. He’s still driving trucks. She asked me where I was and I said Pasco, Washington. She said, “I can send you money or a bus ticket if you need to come back home.” I told her, “No, I’m not leaving until I decide to. I just wanted you all to know that I’m okay.” She said she thought that I might be on the east coast and you’re over there instead. I told her that I’ve already been there before. So, I didn’t come back until I was ready.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You liked what you were doing?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, I got used to going here and there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you ever think that what you were doing was dangerous?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No, not back then. I eventually quit about the same time people started smoking that stuff. They were just starting to do things like that. Every now and then someone would get killed somewhere but I wasn’t nowhere near it. I heard them talk about people killing each other. When I got back, everyone was telling that I wasn’t going to do things like that again, so I quit. I used to just stay with different people. I would stay a week or two, then go stay with someone else. When I was a kid, I was taught that if I stayed with someone then I was to help around the house and work to help pay for my keep. That is how we were taught to do. Also, if someone speaks to you, then you speak to them and not walk away and be rude. They told us that. That’s how we grew up. If there was some kind of event going on, then we couldn’t ask to go with someone if we weren’t asked. They used to tell us that. They raised us good. We were just stubborn sometimes. When we were grown then we did as we pleased.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said there was still land there. Is that allotment land?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I guess so. That was left by my grandpa on dad’s side. We had papers drawn up with all our names on it. On the hill, Oak Ridge.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is it just you and Sam now?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: It’s just me and Sam now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s just you two. So, it’s yours and his now?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: And Nell’s kids.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, and her kids.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: That’s not the only land there. Just down the hill. Do you know Juke Kester?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Where he lives?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: There’s eight of us that has 30 acres straight up the hill. That includes us too. There’s also more around Bell. Seems like 19 acres. There’s supposed to be 20, but someone got the other acre somehow a long time ago, so there’s 19 left. Now eight of us own that. We have four of our family and then the Starrs. Andrew Starr, he raised the girls and they’re included too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are you retired?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What year did you retire?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I quit when I was 63 years old. I started drawing Social Security. They told me I could still work if I wanted to. I told them, “I don’t want to work. That’s why I’m retiring.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s like me. I’m retired, but I work part time. I work on Tuesday and Thursday. What do you do now?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Nothing now. I used to be a mechanic, but I wasn’t certified. I used to work for George Hampton.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You learned on your own?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. George Hampton taught me a lot about fixing cars. They used to have an older Lincoln car. That guy that was the owner of Mid America, chicken fights, he had the car and he loved that car. He and George Hampton brought it over and said he would pay 500 dollars if we could fix it. George said, “Slim, have a look at it.” It took not even 15 minutes to find the problem. I just got lucky. I was looking at the wires and the sensor by the pulley, small sensors like magnets. It was broken into pieces so I took it off. I told George, “I think this is it.” He paid about 60 dollars for the parts, and I put it back together and it started right up. They couldn’t fix before that. George said, “Let’s take it back.” I said, “I’m going to drive it.” He said, “No you’re not.” He wanted to drive it so he could play around with it since it was a nice car. We both had old cars. So, he took off and left me behind, but I knew where he was going. I drove George’s car there. He told that guy, “You’re the one that said it.” So that guy had to pay up. He said, “You all got it fixed real quick.” George pointed to me and said, “He fixed it.” When the man paid up, George got 200 of it and gave me 300. It was late at night when we fixed it and George did help me. We were doing good. George had his own garage.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where was the garage at?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Down the valley near where the Sawneys live. That’s where we were working when he decided to open a pawn shop in Stilwell. He told me I could keep the garage open and used his shop but I said no. I might not be able to repair everything, and I wasn’t pretending to be a smart person. I’ve never thought of myself in that way. Even if you think you know it all, there’s always a wall that will stop you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In everything.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes, I do know that. Then I was just doing whatever after that. I got a good look at what the jails looked like. That was interesting.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you find the best one?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Tahlequah. I stayed in that one for the longest time. I think that may have been the last one that I stayed in. It was better. I stayed in the Sallisaw a few times too. I used to like to make the cops mad. I would race them until they caught me. They would always get me for no license on top of all the other charges. Reckless driving. They liked that one. They would lock me up for that, too. People wanted to bail me out, but I would tell them I was finishing out my time. If they were to bail me out, then I would owe you money for no good reason. If I finish my time, then I would be back on my own again. Sometimes I would go buy another car when I got out. I got to playing with those Tahlequah cops once. There was a one-way bridge over on 82. It was by Greenleaf. That’s where it was. The last time I was messing with them. On the way back, I met a cop and he turned right around and came after me. After I crossed the bridge, I turned my car around. As soon as he came across, I went back across. I went up to the Y and turned around again. We met up right there beside the bridge. We went back and forth until we both got stuck on the bridge. I couldn’t back up because there was another cop behind me. They were just like this. There I was stuck right in the middle.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they tell you to lay down?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No. They just looked at me when I got out of the car. I started looking over the edge of the bridge and they were yelling, “No!” at me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They thought you were going to jump?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. The county guy was walking slowly towards me and talking to me. He was telling me not to jump because you don’t know what’s underneath there. I told him there’s water. He said, “Let’s go. If those other guys take you then they will beat on you.” He said, “I will take you peacefully.” I went with him. Those others probably wanted to beat me up. They locked me up in Tahlequah at the old jail. Now days it’s at a different place somewhere around here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Over there somewhere.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: That was the only jail.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes those cops have a different plan. There’s that boy that they had been looking for a long time. A few days ago, those Cherokee Nation Marshals came to our house. There was a lot of them too. They had dogs and rifles. They even had an ambulance there. They had some bad intentions towards that boy. That boy got away. I believe that boy was taught some things because Diganotsatli was his great grandpa. He was telling us some things later, after they left and gave up looking for him. He said they were using dogs. He said they came as close to him as we are close right now. They didn’t see him.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Daniel is like that. Nell’s kid. Daniel, he’s a twin though. His twin is in jail right now at Stilwell. The other one, he’s just here and there. They were after him that one time when we lived at I told him just turn yourself in. There was a trailer house there too. He said, “Watch this. I’m going to hide. I’ll be back in a little bit.” There were cops walking all over the place. He went down the hill and there was a small stream down there. He said he lay down right there beside the stream and they never found him. They looked all over for him. The cops said, “I guess he got away.” So they left. Later on, he popped up and came walking back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what this boy said and they had a dog.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: These guys didn’t have a dog, just a lot of cops.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They had one of those things they call a drone. It was all over the place.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah. People know things like that. Daniel is a twin though. I was laughing at him that one time about going back to a place he’d been. He was talking about a valley somewhere that had real pretty flowers and grass. It had rocks sticking out of cliffs. He said there was a lot of people standing around. Little People they call them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh yeah?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He said he and Damon would watch them. Damon’s a bonehead. He picked one of the flowers there. As soon as he did that, they saw those Little People pick up rocks. They started throwing them. Boy, it sure stung when they got hit. They took off running then. They had red spots on them where they got hit with rocks. He said the rocks were this big. They threw them hard. They came up on their community, I guess.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He got in trouble for picking a flower?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. They got mad at him for picking a flower. He said there were a lot of those people there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Surprisingly, they didn’t cause them to get lost. They say they can do that to you.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. They saw kids too. They were running by and some were riding lizards. With twins, it’s not always when they can see them. Maybe every month or so. They can see right through people. They hid guns from them once. They asked their dad why he had guns hidden. He kept them in the pickup to hide them because they were Christmas presents for the twins. They just walked by and looked in that direction and went into the house. They asked their dad whose guns those were. He said, “What guns?” “Those you have in the pickup,” they said. They hadn’t seen them and no one knew that he had them in there. They had already seen them when they went in the house. He took them out and gave them to the boys. He told them, “These are yours for Christmas.” They were 22s. They gave them guns every year. When that thing came out then they were gone. They traded for that. I started losing stuff too. I used to have a lot of wrenches. I was missing some of those. I left them there when I moved. I didn’t have any use for them. I can’t do anything now. If I lay down right there, it would take me quite a while to get back up. If I work on a car, then I know what to expect, if I have to go underneath and what wrench to use. I just take one or two and when I get done, I could just leave them there to pick up one at a time. I can’t do that now. I’m crippled up now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you seen Little People?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No, I haven’t but I’ve been close to them before. There used to be some by Cherry Tree. Where the Waters used to live. Over there where Jimmy Ray Livers used to live.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: They lived close to there. Sometimes we would be on the porch, and they would walk by and be talking. We couldn’t see them though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you understand what they were saying?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No. You can’t understand them. They would walk by and go up the hill towards the highway. I had been up that hill before and it’s nice there. They wouldn’t let us go there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Because of the Little People?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. They used to say they could get you and take you with them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes. Do you remember Godawasg? Half brother?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They say they took him once. He was told not to talk about it for seven years. That’s what they told him. He was talking that. He said the chairs were rattlesnakes. That’s where they sat at. He told some very interesting things.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Those boys would go into the snake dens in the winter when it was real cold.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: They said there was a small space and they went in there. They were always told not to go there. When they went in it was like a small room and there were holes on the sides. Some were big and some were small. In between those were mounds of dirt. They said about that big and tall. There were some piles even bigger, just everywhere. I asked those boys if they knew what those piles were. They didn’t know. When the snakes come out and they coil up, that dirt piles up in the middle. They said, “Gah! There’s got to be some huge snakes in there.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Right.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. I used to know where some of those rattlesnakes lived. We used to go watch them. Probably the scariest one I saw, I don’t even know how to describe it, but then I didn’t see all of it either. His tail was that big!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Whoa!

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: His rattles were about this wide and this long!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Wow!

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He was on his way back in when I saw him. There were others laying around about this big. They were laying everywhere. We heard a dog down in the holler and we went that way. Surprisingly, we didn’t step on one because they’re blind at that time of year. I think it’s the month of March when they come out and it warms up. There was a little snow on the ground. We walked in the middle and climbed rocks, and the dog ran that way. There was something going on with the dog. After we got down there, we started looking around. There were snakes all over where we just came from. Rattlesnakes were out sunning themselves. Every now and then we would go watch them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did one of them bite the dog?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. He lived for a while, then he died. He sure was a good squirrel-hunting dog too. Straight across the valley was Hunting Mill Holler. There’s some that live there and another one this side of the holler. It goes around into a valley. If you come in from the other side across from there you can see them about March and April. They come out everywhere then and they’re moving about. I don’t know what the big ones do. That’s where we saw that big one. There’s a cliff and there’s a hole there. There’s a rock sitting there on this side. They told me to go look, so I went in there. I looked in there and there was a rattlesnake sitting right there and it was this big! I went right back out. We killed one of them. I looked at that boy and he said, “Don’t!” He knew what I was going to do. I picked up the dead snake and made those boys run off. I was carrying that snake, but it was dead not alive. We took it with us. It was about six feet long. We used to go all over in the woods growing up. We used to stay with anybody and go kill squirrels. We brought back what we killed. We killed a groundhog once. We didn’t know what it was. I had never seen one before. We found one and took it with us. We were just going to show the elders and ask what it was and they took it away from us. They sure cooked a good meal with it that evening.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you eat it?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it good?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: It was good. We grew up eating things like that. We hunted/foraged in the woods. There were some men that stayed around there, working and making posts. They sold some too. They would bring food too. I don’t know if they made any money, but they had a truck. They made logs too. We did that and helped them. I helped to strip them down, and chopped on them some. There was just one, but there were three of us taking the bark off while they had it supported. When I got off of that one, there would be another waiting for me to start on. That’s what we did as kids. We would come back after they rotated it and do the same thing again. They would measure it off. We just had a good time with it. By afternoon, my arms would be hanging from using an axe.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you make anything?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We didn’t make any money. We were just helping them out so they could buy groceries or whatever they needed. They had hogs too. A lot of people would come if they killed a hog. They didn’t just kill a hog, they would kill three or four. They would give the helpers whatever they wanted of it to take home.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was this all day?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: All day.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was this in the winter?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Just as winter was starting. They did that when they were going to have a big dinner too. I never cut up none of that, though. I did want to cut up some people before. [laughs] I was mad at them. I never got that far though. I would go get wood to make the fire with. They did the rest.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you said earlier that they were wanting to beat you up, were you joking or is it true?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: You mean those cops?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they want to do that?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. The cops wanted to beat me up. That was the last time they locked me up in Tahlequah. What’s that called? I was working for Cherokee Nation. They came to visit me in jail and told me they’d make a deal with me. They could get me out right then and I wouldn’t have to pay. They would help Cherokees if the charges weren’t too serious. Mine wasn’t that bad, just when I was messing with them that one time. He told me if I went to rehab, he would get me out. I asked where at and he said Miami. I asked him what I would do. He said I would be there for three months and then come back, go to court and that would make it easier on me. He said if you stay here, then you’ll go to jail or prison and I had a choice to make. I said I would go to rehab. He got me out and took me to where Jerry lived. He told me not to run away. They told him that I was not running away. He came to get me on Monday and we left. I was there four months. I was supposed to be there for three, but they said I needed to stay another month. I had counselors there in rehab. I had to go to court, and they dropped some of the charges and said I would need to pay 400 dollars. There was nothing wrong with that. I turned around and they didn’t lock me up. When I did get out, I would go to all my court dates. When I left and was walking down the street, I saw Johnny Christie coming.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: From Tahlequah?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. He asked me if I needed a job and I said yes. He said he would hire me. He worked for Cherokee Nation then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you already driving a backhoe then?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No. I had quit driving it long before that. He asked me if I could run a backhoe. I told him if they need me to. I would have to play around with it some to get used to one again. He did the same job at Tahlequah. Somewhere in Tahlequah there’s a church that sits in a low area and it’s a Cherokee Church. That’s where we laid the cable close by. I forgot the name of the church. I know it’s in Tahlequah. We buried some telephone lines on a hill somewhere. We went to Stigler after that. I paid off my 400 dollars doing that. After that I went to Sallisaw and got put in jail again. I told them that I fell off the wagon. It was later before I quit drinking and getting into trouble. They eventually let me go though. I think they were after someone else and I got in the way. I was in there for a short time. Johnny Christie and I went to Stigler. We stayed about three months and Johnny got sick. It was there when he started having constant pain. I told him to quit, and he asked me what I was going to do. I told him that I would find something else. He had cancer right here. That’s what killed him. He had a lot of equipment but that boy, Thomas, got it all. He didn’t do anything with it because it was all leased. So, it was all taken back. I don’t know what Thomas did. He died about three or four years later. I don’t know what happened. There’s one boy left and he wasn’t good for anything. We also came to Woodall and worked there, laying down telephone lines. I was using a different kind of machine to dig with, not a backhoe. There was an old man that came and asked me what I was doing. I told him, “There’s a water line under here somewhere.” I was looking for it before I start digging because I don’t want to break it. He said, “You won’t find it with that. They put that water line in a long time ago. They put a lot of gravel in there about five or six years ago. It’s about this deep where you’re digging.”[?] He might have said 10 feet deep for the water line. He said you can’t hurt it. He said, “How deep are you going to dig?” I said, “Two feet.” He said, “Go ahead and dig.” I didn’t hit anything while digging. There was a small bridge there, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you find it?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We didn’t dig after that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No, it went across and we were working on the side of it. We went on but we had to watch for water lines. The water department used to come out and put those things out there. You can find the water lines yourself and you don’t have to use a machine. I learned that. You can get a wire clothes hanger and bend it and do it like this and do like this where it’s bent. You start walking and if there’s a water line these will meet.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: You can find a water line.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Or water.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: And water. Not sure about just water. That’s what we did to find water lines. The Indian way they said. Johnny Christie taught me that. He was knowledgeable. I think he was Ned Christie’s grandson.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He knew a lot of things. His brother’s name was Walter. He was a heavy drinker and a mean man. He went to Illinois and became a preacher. I had asked someone what became of Walter, and they told me he became a preacher. He died not too long ago. He has family somewhere. I don’t know them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you do now?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Nothing. Just watch people. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don’t go fishing?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No, not now, but I used to. There was Gowen, Calvin Soap. We used to go all the time. He got sick, too. We’d go all the time, but I can’t do that now. I can’t go to the lake and sit down to fish.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then you could go to the river.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes, I could. We would go there and get quite a lot and then we would take them home and clean them right where I live right now. One time Calvin, Billy, and I, had come back, and we had a pile of fish. Calvin was cooking them. Then someone came. They were looking for Cherokee speakers. It was someone named Pettit and two women. There was another man because there were four of them. I already had one of those things that they were handing out. I got one at Greasy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That necklace?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes, I already had one from there. Calvin and Billy didn’t have one because they were afraid to get one. When they came, we told them to eat. They couldn’t resist and ate some fish. We didn’t even eat them all. There was some left. That’s the way elders were. Diganotsatli, the one you was talking about?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The one that lived by Greasy.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We used to go to his house when we were boys. We used to like to listen to them joke around with people and liked to listen to them. As soon as we got there, that old lady would go in the kitchen. You couldn’t say no to them because they would whip you if you were to say no. [laughs] You were going to eat if you went to visit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There was always a lot of people there.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Always.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you too young to join in the card games?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Playing cards.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t join in?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No, I didn’t play cards.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: They were throwing dice one time. I took all their money. They were mad because they wanted to keep their money. I threw out two dollars and they gave it back to me. I was sitting all by myself later on with a pile of money. They were mad at me! I had never thrown them before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you know Tsusolvd?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He said they were playing with his dad once. His dad was, how would you say that? Conjuring? He was blowing on them while he was holding them. Someone noticed that and said, “Hey, that old man is conjuring those.” They said, “Ha! He just cold!” [laughs]

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: They were funny and it was a good place to visit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: A long time ago, that Ross was a good place to visit too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes. You know Whitey don’t you?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. There were good places to visit everywhere I went. I was always by myself. It might have been better if I had someone with me. Then maybe I’m better by myself in case I did something bad and they could have turned me in. I could do whatever I wanted by myself.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said you went everywhere. Where is the farthest you ever been?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Spokane, Washington.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Over there?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I guess you could say that. It’s way in the corner. Northeast, it’s Northwest.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you ride a train once or more than that?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: There were others, but I forget them all.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: It was a long way though. But the farthest, those boys, where did they say? Those Nofire boys said if we catch a train, we can be back at Stilwell in no time. So, they got in the box car. The train drove right through Stilwell doing about 60 m.p.h. [laughs] They finally got off at Marble City, and they had to walk back. Some of them go real fast. There’s one in Texas, but I can’t remember what they call it. You can really hear that one. It goes about 200 m.p.h. It goes from New Mexico to Arizona. We were on a mountain close by there and we were waiting on it. We weren’t going to get on it. We could hear it coming a long way off. Jeeeeeeee! You could hear the wheels! It wasn’t the motor. It sounded like it was right over us and sparks were flying everywhere. It went past real quick! I don’t know if they still run those. It wouldn’t be able to stop fast if there happened to be something in its path. I don’t know where it comes from, maybe Houston. Galveston was a good place to visit too. I’ve been there before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you went to New Mexico, were there Mexicans or white people?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: They were Indians. A lot of them and others mixed in. There were many Indians there, Hopis and different ones.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did you stay there?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: New Mexico?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Probably four months. We were in the desert part. They were putting up telephone poles. You can’t dig a hole out there because it’s so dry. They had to use a digging machine and as soon as you dig a hole, it fills back up with sand. They would pour water on a big area before digging. If they dug about five feet, it had to be wet or damp. They would put the pole up real fast. We would fill it back up then when it dried…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It would harden?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you pick up any of the Mexican’s language?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Huh? A long time ago. Not much really, just some bad words. [laughs] Words that could get me in trouble. They did that to George once. George Hampton. There was a guy that he ran around with, Dayudsin was his Cherokee name. They went over to Diganotsatli’s old place. They had him say something that wasn’t nice. George didn’t know any Cherokee and he said it to some woman. When he got back in the car he said as soon as we’re out of sight, I’m going to beat you up! I don’t know what he asked for? [laughs] Sam used to speak Spanish a long time ago.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Had he been there too?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No, he lived in Texas though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: He was working around turkeys somewhere in Texas. There were lots of Mexicans working there and they didn’t understand English or Cherokee, so he had to learn the language. There was one that spoke English and he taught Sam to speak Spanish. He just kept learning and he was able to speak pretty good. He may have forgotten how to by now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you all still see each other? Sam?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. We watch out for each other now. We weren’t close before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In the past?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It all changed?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: Yes. Not until we were adults.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: We used to beat on each other.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who had the upper hand?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I could push him around in the beginning. Then he learned Karate. I told him it doesn’t matter what you do, I can still beat you! He wouldn’t come after me, but he would other people. He told me I could learn it too, but I told him that I didn’t want to. He asked me why I didn’t want to, and I said, “Because I might go after you if I learned it.” He said, “It’s just for your protection and defense. You can let things go unless they start pushing you around then you defend yourself. They will teach you that.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: To kill someone?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: No. That you don’t have to fight back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just to make you stronger.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: You have to keep moving away as long as you can because you can kill them real quick if you hit them in the right spot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I told him that I’m that way. If I killed someone it would be intentional. [laughs] We just didn’t get along at the time. We’ve been around a lot, but we kept an eye on each other in case of a disagreement. Now days, we just share all the memories. He lost one of his girls recently.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, true.

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I really loved that girl. She was the youngest. She would come right over as soon as she saw me. The others aren’t that way. We speak to each other, but not like her. There was no doubt that she would come to talk to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We’re finishing up now. I’m going to ask you the same question that you were asked the last time. What do you think is going to become of the Cherokee Language like we have been speaking today?

segments.speaker: harry-daugherty
segments.translation: I’m going to say what I said to the last person. We are going to trade or switch languages. The white people are learning to speak Cherokee. I have spoken with several white people that are able to carry on a good conversation in Cherokee. The Cherokees are loudly speaking English.
